name: Beth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 58, and I'm a troubleshooter for the electricity company, which means I'm the one person in a truck who gets sent first when the power goes out, to find the problem and fix it or call in a crew. I cover the edge of town and the farm roads beyond it. My husband Tom and I have forty acres and a small herd of beef cattle, which he runs while I work. We've got a daughter, Anna, who's a dental hygienist, and a son, Mark, who's a mechanic, and two grandchildren.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work a rotation, so some weeks it's days and some weeks I'm on call nights. When the phone goes at 3am, I'm in the truck in ten minutes, find the blown fuse or the downed wire, make it safe, and get people's lights back. I love being the one who shows up, people come out in their dressing gowns and thank you. What wears me out now is the night weeks, I don't bounce back like I used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a helpful tool and nothing to lose sleep over. I'd say that at church, at the feed store, wherever people ask. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going till 62, like we planned. Tom and I would keep the cattle, and I'd maybe go part-time for the last year if they let me. That's all good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep the savings, which is about three months' worth plus the farm, though the farm barely pays for itself. Keep helping with the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the company use any AI in your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an outage map now that guesses where the fault is, from which customers called in. It's right maybe two times out of three, which is handy. I check it, then I drive the line anyway, because the map doesn't know about the old oak by the creek.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your next few years look like if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mentor the two new troubleshooters, Josh and Kayla, so they're ready for nights on their own. Then retire, help Tom with the herd, and see the grandkids more. Maybe teach Sunday school again.

S0.say: She'd say it's a helpful tool and nothing to lose sleep over, at church or at the feed store, wherever people ask. She doesn't post online.
S0.think: It means she keeps going until 62 as planned, maybe part-time in the last year, while she and Tom keep the cattle. That's all good with her.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal, with about three months of savings plus a small farm that barely pays for itself. Keeps helping train the apprentices.
S0.quote: I check it, then I drive the line anyway, because the map doesn't know about the old oak by the creek.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is a troubleshooter who works alone, often at night, and loves being the one who shows up. She uses the outage map but trusts her own knowledge of the land more. Her farm is part of her identity but not much of a financial cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like when the company brought in the mobile computers in the trucks. People grumbled, then they got used to it. Learn what you need and keep doing good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. You can't fix a downed line at 3am with a computer. But the tools would get better at finding faults, and that might mean fewer troubleshooters on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up the better tools once the other troubleshooters had tried them and they'd proved themselves. I'd go on the company training. And I'd keep my eye on the roster, if they started cutting shifts, I'd want to know early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones who've just come in, Josh and Kayla. If there are fewer troubleshooter jobs, they'll be the ones squeezed. And the call centre girls, because a program could answer those calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go further with the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's proven, yes. I already ask a chatbot now and then to explain a new procedure in plain words, it's quicker than ringing the office. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last either.

S1.say: She'd compare it to when the company brought mobile computers into the trucks: people grumbled, then got used to it. Learn what you need and keep doing good work.
S1.think: She thinks she'd be fine because nobody fixes a downed line at 3am with a computer. But better fault-finding tools might mean fewer troubleshooters on the roster.
S1.do: Picks up better tools once other troubleshooters have proven them and goes on company training. Keeps an eye on the roster so she hears early if shifts are cut.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little watchful.
S1.quote: You can't fix a downed line at 3am with a computer.
S1.fieldNote: She sees this as another round of new kit, like the truck computers, and expects to adapt once tools are proven. Her quiet worry is the roster and the young troubleshooters she's mentoring. She already uses a chatbot to put procedures in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is happening too fast for families and towns to cope, and the companies doing it should slow down. I'd say people need to pull together, families, churches, neighbours. I don't think government cheques fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. I'd be 60, two years short of retirement, and if a robot truck can find and fix a fault, they don't need me driving out at 3am. Three months of savings doesn't stretch far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder now, no new truck, no trip to see Tom's sister. I'd talk to Tom about selling more of the beef straight to people in town, a bit of extra money every month. If the company had any role watching over the robots, I'd put my hand up, once I saw it actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but my stomach drops when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Josh and Kayla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn every bit of the new equipment and to hold on to the parts of the job that need a person, like talking to scared customers. And to look after each other. The company won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lean on it more. Tom's been wanting to sell boxes of beef to families in town for years, and I've always said we didn't need the bother. If my job went, we'd need the bother.

S2.say: She'd say it's happening too fast for families and towns to cope, that the companies doing it should slow down and that families, churches and neighbours need to pull together. She doesn't think government cheques fix it.
S2.think: It scares her: she'd be 60, two years short of retirement, and a robot truck that can find and fix faults means nobody needs her driving out at 3am. Three months of savings doesn't stretch far.
S2.do: Saves harder, dropping a new truck and a family trip, and works with Tom on selling beef directly to families in town for extra monthly income. Volunteers for any robot-supervising role once it's proven to work.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her stomach dropping, though not panicking.
S2.quote: If my job went, we'd need the bother.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline would leave her two years short with thin savings, and her answer is the farm and community rather than the state. She'd still try a robot-watching role, but only once it's proven. Her advice to the young troubleshooters was protective and a little bitter about the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it sensibly. Companies should keep training their people and keep the apprenticeships going. Families should plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63, so I'd be just past my retirement when it arrives. That makes a big difference. I'd be mostly out of it, as long as they don't start cutting early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving a bit more and get the beef boxes going slowly, so it's an established thing by the time I retire. I'd learn the newer tools once they'd been tested on other districts. And I'd help Josh and Kayla plan, so they're not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years let you do, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the side business going properly, not in a panic. Rebuild the savings. Retire on time. With two years it's a scramble, with five it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your kids about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Mark's a mechanic, and robots can fix cars too, eventually. I'd tell him to keep learning the new systems, electric cars and all that, and that his dad and I will help with the grandkids if he needs to retrain.

S3.say: She'd say there's time, so use it sensibly: companies should keep training people and keep apprenticeships going, and families should plan ahead.
S3.think: She'd be 63 and just past retirement when it arrives, which makes a big difference. She'd be mostly out of it as long as cuts don't start early.
S3.do: Saves a bit more and builds up the beef box sales slowly so they're established by retirement. Learns newer tools once tested on other districts and helps her young troubleshooters plan.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: With two years it's a scramble, with five it's a plan.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn her scramble into a plan: side business, savings, retire on time. Her worry broadens to her son, a mechanic. She'd offer childcare support so he could retrain, which fits her family-first values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people to get ready if they work at it. Learn a trade, look after your family, and don't count on anyone else to do it for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired by then, I'd be 68 and with the cattle. So for me it's fine. It's the grandkids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am and retire at 62. Use the new tools when they come and they're proven. Keep the farm ticking over and maybe grow the beef side for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit wistful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to work with their hands and their heads, and to be someone people can count on. Whatever the jobs are, people still need someone who shows up. I'd want them to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss if machines took over the night calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thank-yous. An old man on Ridge Road brought me a slice of pie at 4am once, after I'd got his power back in a snowstorm. A robot won't get the pie.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough time for people to get ready if they work at it: learn a trade, look after your family and don't count on anyone else to do it for you.
S4.think: She'll be 68, retired and with the cattle, so it's fine for her. Her thoughts go to her grandchildren.
S4.do: Keeps working as she is and retires at 62, using new tools once proven. Keeps the farm going and may grow the beef side for retirement.
S4.quote: A robot won't get the pie.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's calm and her focus is the grandchildren. Her wistfulness is about the human moments of the job, like the pie at 4am. Self-reliance and family come through as her core values in every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it lands two years before I'm done, and three months of savings won't cover that. What would help is the company giving older workers a fair way to finish, maybe moving us onto watching the robots, and keeping the apprenticeships going for the young ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely it gets. When the power's out, it's me and a flashlight on a dark road, and people are scared. Part of my job is just being a calm voice at the door. I hope whatever comes still has someone to knock on the door.

headlineQuote: Part of my job is just being a calm voice at the door.
portrait: Beth Kowalski is a 58-year-old troubleshooter who works alone in a truck, often at night, getting people's power back on the edge of town while her husband Tom runs their small beef herd. She uses tools like the outage map once they've proven themselves, but trusts her own knowledge of the land more. She stays calm through the plateau and steady change, becomes anxious with AGI by 2028 because she'd be two years short of retirement with three months of savings, and turns to the farm, saving and community rather than government. With five or ten years she builds a beef box sideline, retires on time and thinks about her children and grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would land two years before she's done and her three months of savings wouldn't cover it.
whatWouldHelp: A fair way for older workers to finish, such as moving them onto supervising robots, and keeping apprenticeships going for young people.
